case_name: Revlon, Inc. v. MacAndrews & Forbes Holdings, Inc.
key_holding: When the sale of a company becomes inevitable, the role of directors shifts from corporate defenders to auctioneers charged with getting the best price for stockholders.
substantive_analysis: The Delaware Supreme Court affirmed that lock-up options, no-shop provisions, and cancellation fees that end an active bidding contest without providing commensurate value to shareholders breach the fiduciary duty of loyalty under heightened scrutiny.

citable_spans.text: The duty of the board had thus changed from the preservation of Revlon as a corporate entity to the maximization of the company's value at a sale for the stockholders' benefit.
A lock-up is not per se illegal under Delaware law... but when bidders make relatively similar offers, or dissolution of the company becomes inevitable, the auction must continue.

case_name: In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation
key_holding: Directors possess an affirmative fiduciary obligation to assure that an adequate corporate information and reporting system exists reasonably designed to provide timely, accurate information to senior management.
substantive_analysis: Chancellor Allen articulated that a sustained or systematic failure of the board to exercise oversight—such as an utter failure to attempt to assure a reasonable information and reporting system exists—establishes the lack of good faith that is a necessary condition to board oversight liability.

citable_spans.text: A director's obligation includes a duty to attempt in good faith to assure that a corporate information and reporting system, which the board concludes is adequate, exists.

case_name: G.A. Stowers Furniture Co. v. American Indemnity Co.
key_holding: An insurer defending a third-party liability claim owes a duty of ordinary care to settle within policy limits when a reasonably prudent insurer would do so in light of the exposure.
substantive_analysis: Establishes the Texas Stowers Doctrine: where liability is reasonably clear, damages exceed policy limits, and an unconditional offer to release within policy limits is presented, refusal to settle exposes the insurer to full extra-contractual liability for excess judgments.

citable_spans.text: The insurer is held to that degree of care and diligence which an ordinarily prudent person would exercise in the management of his own business.

case_name: Crisci v. Security Insurance Co. of New Haven
key_holding: An insurer that breaches the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing by unreasonably refusing a settlement offer within policy limits is liable for all compensatory damages, including emotional distress.
substantive_analysis: Chief Justice Traynor held that the test for whether a settlement offer within limits must be accepted is whether a prudent insurer without policy limits would have accepted the settlement offer. The insurer cannot gamble with the financial solvency of the insured.

citable_spans.text: Liability is imposed not for a bad faith breach of contract but for failure to meet the duty to accept reasonable settlements, a duty included within the implied covenant of good faith.

case_name: Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_holding: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 supersedes the Frye 'general acceptance' test, assigning the trial judge a gatekeeping role to ensure expert scientific testimony rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant to the task at hand.
substantive_analysis: The Supreme Court outlined five non-exclusive factors: whether the methodology can be and has been tested, peer review and publication, known or potential rate of error, standards controlling the technique's operation, and general acceptance within the relevant scientific community.

citable_spans.text: Faced with a proffer of expert scientific testimony, the trial judge must determine at the outset whether the expert is proposing to testify to (1) scientific knowledge that (2) will assist the trier of fact.

key_holding: In strict products liability design defect and failure-to-warn claims, the state-of-the-art defense (that the danger was undiscoverable at the time of manufacture) is legally unavailable.
substantive_analysis: The court held that in strict liability, the manufacturer's knowledge is imputed as a matter of law. The focus of the inquiry is on the product itself, not on the culpability or scientific limitations of the manufacturer at the time of distribution.

citable_spans.text: In strict liability cases, culpability is irrelevant. The product was unsafe; that is enough.

citation: 119 Cal. App. 3d 757, 174 Cal. Rptr. 348 (Cal. Ct. App. 1981)
key_holding: Corporate management's conscious decision to place a motor vehicle into the stream of commerce knowing that its fuel tank design exposed occupants to catastrophic burn injuries constitutes malice justifying punitive damages.
substantive_analysis: The court affirmed the landmark Ford Pinto verdict, establishing that institutional cost-benefit balancing that trades known human life risks against internal manufacturing cost savings satisfies the statutory standard for malice.

citable_spans.text: There was ample evidence that Ford's conduct was egregious in the extreme... to allow a corporation to trade human lives for economic savings without punitive consequence would make mockery of strict liability.

court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_holding: Establishes the 'fraud-on-the-market' doctrine, providing a rebuttable presumption of investor reliance on corporate misstatements in efficient securities trading markets under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5.
substantive_analysis: Justice Blackmun reasoned that because market professionals rely on the integrity of the market price, an investor who trades stock at the price set by the market does so in reliance on the integrity of that price.

citable_spans.text: The fraud-on-the-market theory is based on the hypothesis that, in an open and developed securities market, the price of a company's stock is determined by the available material information.

court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_holding: An offering of securities to employees or private parties is not exempt from registration under Section 4(a)(1) unless the offerees have access to the same kind of information that registration would disclose. The burden of proof to establish any exemption from Section 5 registration rests strictly upon the issuer and distributor claiming it.
substantive_analysis: The Supreme Court established that the statutory policy of the Securities Act is to protect investors by promoting full disclosure. Because the registration requirement is the central protection of the 1933 Act, exemptions are strictly construed against the claimant. A seller cannot escape strict Section 5 liability without proving every element of an available affirmative exemption.

citable_spans.text: Keeping in mind the statutory policy of protecting investors by promoting full disclosure of information thought necessary to informed investment decisions, the burden of proof is on the one who claims the exemption.

court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_holding: Dissemination of false or misleading statements with intent to deceive can fall within the scope of Rule 10b-5(a) and (c), as well as Section 17(a)(1), even if the disseminator is not the 'maker' of the misstatements under Janus Capital Group. Scheme liability applies broadly to participants in fraudulent securities distribution chains.
substantive_analysis: The Supreme Court resolved circuit tension regarding the boundary between misstatement liability under Rule 10b-5(b) and scheme liability under subsections (a) and (c). The Court held that transmitting misleading statements to investors or facilitating deceptive conduits constitutes employing a 'device, scheme, or artifice to defraud.'

citable_spans.text: By sending emails he understood to contain material untruths, Lorenzo 'employed' a 'device, scheme, or artifice to defraud' within the meaning of subsection (a) and engaged in an 'act, practice, or course of business' that operated as a fraud under subsection (c).

court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
category: Section 5 Strict Liability / Transfer Agent Legend Removal Schemes
key_holding: Section 5 of the Securities Act imposes strict liability for the unregistered offer or sale of securities. Scienter and negligence are not elements of a prima facie Section 5 violation. Facilitators, attorneys, and promoters who are substantial factors or necessary participants in a transfer agent legend removal scheme are strictly liable.
substantive_analysis: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment against participants in a massive microcap distribution scheme where billions of shares were issued without registration through fraudulent attorney opinion letters and transfer agent directives. The court reaffirmed that good faith belief in an exemption is not a defense to Section 5 liability.

citable_spans.text: Section 5 is a strict liability statute. To establish a prima facie violation, the SEC must show that: (1) no registration statement was in effect; (2) the defendant directly or indirectly sold or offered to sell securities; and (3) the sale or offer was made through interstate commerce.

case_name: Wells Fargo Bank v. Arizona Laborers Teamsters
category: Civil Conspiracy / Aiding & Abetting Commercial Fraud
key_holding: A party who knows that another's conduct constitutes a breach of duty and gives substantial assistance or encouragement to the other to so conduct himself is liable for aiding and abetting fraud and civil conspiracy. Knowledge of the fraudulent scheme can be inferred from circumstantial evidence and commercial irregularities.
substantive_analysis: The Arizona Supreme Court established the comprehensive standard for civil conspiracy and aiding and abetting fraud in multi-party commercial and financial schemes. The court held that participants who provide conduits, banking mechanisms, or concealment cannot avoid liability by claiming ignorance of the primary tortfeasor's underlying intent.

citable_spans.text: Claims of aiding and abetting fraud have three elements: (1) the primary tortfeasor must commit a tort; (2) the defendant must know that this conduct constitutes a breach of duty; and (3) the defendant must substantially assist or encourage the primary tortfeasor.
